maria: quick note — I pushed a small experiment for hit-priority enqueue + debounce timer to reduce batch fragmentation when prefix cache hits are frequent. initial numbers look good for overall throughput but short-sequence p99 went up slightly.

ajay: what's the admission rule you used?

maria: pasted version of the admission logic:
```
# simplified admission pseudocode
if request.kv_hit:
  request.priority += 1  # prefer packing hits together
per_batch_token_target = min(global_token_budget - in_flight_tokens, per_request_max)
# debounce: wait up to debounce_ms for extra hits before forming batch
if queue_wait_ms < debounce_ms and can_fill_with_hits():
  wait(debounce_ms - queue_wait_ms)
else:
  flush_batch()
```

kyle: got it. did you tune the token_budget target? if many hits we can safely increase token budget per batch, but that changes kernel selection tradeoffs.

maria: yes — global_token_budget=1024 right now. per_batch_target uses a hit_factor: per_batch = max(128, min(remaining, 512 * hit_factor)). with hit_factor=2 we pack more tokens for hits. interestingly that made the runtime pick kernel_b more often which is slightly slower for short seqs.

elaine: can you drop the profiler output or flamegraph? and which kernel selection policy are we using?

maria: flamegraph: (uploaded to run artifacts) https://ci.internal/artifacts/rrun/1887/flame.svg 
kernel selection today: if avg_seq_len > 256 -> kernel_b else kernel_a. problem: with high kv_hit batches avg_seq_len falls but effective compute per token also falls — so kernel_b sometimes beats kernel_a despite shorter seqs because memory vs compute balance shifts.

ajay: suggestion: compute an estimated cost that accounts for hit_rate. e.g.
```
est_cost = cpu_cost + (1 - hit_rate) * gpu_cost_est
choose kernel with lower est_cost
```
This will bias toward kernels that favor memory-bound vs compute-bound behavior depending on hit_rate.

kyle: relatedly, queue ordering matters. We saw misses getting starved when hits were preferred. maybe use deadline-based ordering with a secondary hit-priority so misses don't get arbitrarily delayed.

maria: implemented a quick deadline slotting prototype: assign deadline = now + SLO_ms - est_proc_ms, then sort queue by (deadline, -hit_priority). Early results: miss tail drops ~12% while hit throughput stays ~+6%.

ci-bot: Perf CI: canary run 2028-11-01 completed. Observed p99 short-seq latency +8% (regression), p50/p95 roughly same. Full logs: https://ci.internal/1234

elaine: ok, assign to @ajay and @kyle to iterate on kernel cost model + queue policy. please run microprofs for mixes: 60% hits (seqs 32) / 40% misses (seqs 512) and also 80/20 and 20/80. include KV cache warm/cold scenarios.

ajay: on it — will run microprof with synthetic mix and post results in ~1h :hourglass_flowing_sand:

kyle: if ajay is running tests I can add a variant that uses per-batch kernel selection (evaluate switching cost) vs per-request selection. also try reducing debounce_ms from 8ms -> 3ms to see tail impact.

maria: thanks — rough checklist so we don't forget:
- run microprof mixes (ajay)
- add estimated-cost kernel selector (kyle)
- run canary with deadline-slotting enabled (maria)
- simulate cold KV cache to ensure we don't just overfit to warmed hits (everyone)

maria: quick FYI — noticed an odd micro-regression: when hit-heavy batches pack many short requests we increase kernel launch overhead. adding a micro-batcher that coalesces kernels reduced that overhead by ~1-2ms. will benchmark more. :thumbsup:
